<a id="ingredient-identity-and-scope"></a>
## What counts as grapes

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-003"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-can-be-transferred-between-those-materials-and-what-requires-a-separate-answer"></a>

This page covers grapes in 6 forms kept separate in every comparison: grapes, as sold (686 results), grapes, peeled or flesh (77 results), grapes, dried (15 results), grapes, oil (12 results), grapes, <div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-grapes" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-grapes-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of grapes, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>79</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>FDA Total Diet Study</td><td>27</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Sembratowicz et al. 2010</td><td>2</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Spungen et al. 2024</td><td>1</td><td>25%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for grapes, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>4 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Li et al. 2018</td><td>1</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for grapes, peeled or flesh on a dry weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>Li et al. 2018 is the only compatible sampling family for grapes, peeled or flesh on this basis in the completed grapes ledger, so this single-family reference cannot represent other markets. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach grapes

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach grapes comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Grapes, as sold from processed product, Poland retail/official control had lead higher at 70 µg/kg, against 5 µg/kg for fresh product, Poland retail/official control in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rusin M, Domagalska J, Rogala D, Razzaghi M, Szymala I · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Concentration of cadmium and lead in vegetables and fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, grapes, as sold from microwave-cooked 10 min had nickel higher at 4,430 µg/kg, against 361 µg/kg for boiled 15 min at 102 C in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/sundhar2023-gulf-mannar-seaweed-metals|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Sundhar S, Shakila RJ, Shalini R, Aanand S, Jayakumar N · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/sundhar2023-gulf-mannar-seaweed-metals">Effect of thermal processing on toxic heavy metals in edible seaweeds of Gulf of Mannar and their health risk assessment</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Regional Studies in Marine Science</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/sundhar2023-gulf-mannar-seaweed-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, grapes, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (4.85 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (275 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (8.5 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (11 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

## Processing, cooking and preparation

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-017"></a>
<a id="how-do-derivatives-concentrates-extracts-and-fractions-differ-from-their-parent-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-018"></a>
<a id="do-changes-reflect-removal-redistribution-moisture-or-yield-change-dilution-or-altered-species-or-availability"></a>

Processed or prepared forms were compared only with unprocessed grapes in the same study and group. Grapes, peeled or flesh (all samples) had lead higher at 370 µg/kg, against 240 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (grapes, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li X, Dong S, Su X · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Copper and other heavy metals in grapes: a pilot study tracing influential factors and evaluating potential risks in China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports (2018) 8:17407</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.

<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rusin M, Domagalska J, Rogala D, Razzaghi M, Szymala I · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Concentration of cadmium and lead in vegetables and fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-grapes" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-grapes" data-question="How do heavy metals get into grapes?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into grapes?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, grapes from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than grapes from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rusin M, Domagalska J, Rogala D, Razzaghi M, Szymala I · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Concentration of cadmium and lead in vegetables and fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Grapes, as sold from processed product, Poland retail/official control had lead higher at 70 µg/kg, against 5 µg/kg for fresh product, Poland retail/official control in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rusin M, Domagalska J, Rogala D, Razzaghi M, Szymala I · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Concentration of cadmium and lead in vegetables and fruits</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rusin2021-vegetables-fruits-cadmium-lead-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, grapes, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (4.85 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (275 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (8.5 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (11 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same grapes.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li X, Dong S, Su X · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Copper and other heavy metals in grapes: a pilot study tracing influential factors and evaluating potential risks in China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports (2018) 8:17407</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Grapes, peeled or flesh (all samples) had lead higher at 370 µg/kg, against 240 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (grapes, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li X, Dong S, Su X · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Copper and other heavy metals in grapes: a pilot study tracing influential factors and evaluating potential risks in China</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports (2018) 8:17407</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2018-china-grapes-copper-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-grapes-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-grapes-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in grapes is inorganic?">
